notes.meaning: Daniel receives a second vision in the third year of King Belshazzar, about two years after his first vision. The language of the book changes back to Hebrew here because the message centers directly on God's chosen people, Israel. God gave this revelation to show what major kingdom changes would happen before the Messiah came.

In this vision, Daniel sees himself transported to the citadel of Susa by the Ulai Canal in the province of Elam. Susa was a fortified royal city that would later become a grand capital of the Persian Empire. This setting showed Daniel the very place where the next world power would rise and rule.

Daniel looks up and sees a ram standing beside the canal with two long horns, representing the Medo-Persian Empire. One horn was longer than the other and grew up later, showing how Persia rose after Media and became the dominant partner. Persian rulers even carried the emblem of a ram into battle.

The ram charges west, north, and south, conquering lands in every direction with irresistible strength. Persia conquered Babylon, Egypt, and parts of Asia Minor, while making few conquests to the east. The ram acted proudly and did whatever it pleased, yet it operated entirely within God's sovereign plan.

Suddenly, a male goat with a single prominent horn between its eyes comes charging out of the west so fast that its feet do not touch the ground. This goat represents the Greek Empire, and its notable horn represents its first great king, Alexander the Great. Alexander marched his armies across the earth with incredible speed, conquering the Persian world in only a few years.

The goat rushes directly at the two-horned ram beside the canal with furious power. This describes Greece launching a military strike against the Persian Empire to pay it back for past invasions. Alexander attacked Persia with intense wrath and unmatched determination.

In great anger, the goat strikes the ram, shatters both of its horns, and knocks it to the ground to trample it. Alexander crushed the Persian armies in decisive battles, and no nation could rescue the Persian empire from his grasp. The once mighty kingdom was completely overthrown by Greece.

The goat grew extremely powerful, but at the very height of its strength, the large horn was suddenly broken off. Alexander died unexpectedly at age thirty-three, leaving no single heir to keep his vast empire together. In place of that single horn, four notable horns grew out toward the four winds, representing four kingdoms ruled by his top generals.

Out of one of the four kingdoms comes a little horn that expands toward the south, the east, and the Beautiful Land of Israel. This horn represents Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a ruler from the Syrian branch who took the throne through bribery and deceit. He turned his cruel attention directly against Judea and the Jewish people.

The little horn grows so tall that it reaches the host of heaven, throwing some of the stars to the earth and trampling on them. This symbolic picture describes Antiochus persecuting God's holy people and their leaders, who are pictured as shining stars. He attacked the faithful community and tried to crush their faith.

The horn exalts itself against the Prince of the host, who is God Himself. Antiochus attacked the worship of God by stopping the daily morning and evening sacrifices and desecrating the holy temple in Jerusalem. By turning God's house into a pagan shrine, he openly defied the Lord of heaven.

Because of the sinful rebellion among the people, the holy temple and the regular sacrifices were handed over to this tyrant. He threw truth to the ground by outlawing God's laws and burning sacred scrolls. For an appointed season, his wicked plans seemed to succeed everywhere.

Daniel hears two holy angels talking with one another about the vision. One angel asks how long this terrible desecration will last and how long the temple and God's people will be trampled down. Even the angels in heaven were deeply concerned about the suffering of God's sanctuary.

The holy one replies that the suffering will last for 2,300 evenings and mornings before the sanctuary is properly restored. This timeframe marked the period of Antiochus's persecution, ending when the temple was cleansed and rededicated by faithful Jews. God set a definite boundary on how long the hardship could endure.

differ.view: The 2,300 evenings and mornings are literal natural days fulfilled during the historical persecution under Antiochus.
The days are prophetic years, pointing to a much longer span of history across twenty-three centuries.
The number refers to literal days under Antiochus, but can also foreshadow years pointing toward the end times.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some prophetic movements interpreted the 2,300 days as 2,300 years that culminated in the year 1844.

notes.meaning: As Daniel tried to understand what he had seen, someone with the appearance of a man suddenly stood in front of him. This heavenly being took on human form so Daniel could receive the explanation. Daniel recognized that he needed divine assistance to make sense of the revelation.

Daniel hears a human voice calling out from between the banks of the Ulai canal, ordering Gabriel to explain the vision. This voice carried divine authority because it had the power to direct a holy angel. This is the very first time in Scripture that a holy angel is mentioned by name.

When Gabriel approached, Daniel was so terrified that he collapsed facedown on the ground. The angel addressed him as "son of man" to remind Daniel of his human weakness compared to the glory of heaven. Gabriel told him that the vision points toward the appointed time of the end.

differ.view: The time of the end refers to the final period of the Old Testament era before Christ, fulfilled under Antiochus.
The time of the end refers to the final days of human history before Christ returns, when the ultimate Antichrist appears.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Early church fathers like Jerome taught that the events under Antiochus serve as a pattern and forerunner for what the final Antichrist will do at the end of history.

notes.meaning: While Gabriel spoke, Daniel fell into a deep swoon with his face pressed to the ground. The overwhelming glory of the heavenly messenger was more than human weakness could bear. Gabriel then touched Daniel and helped him stand upright so he could hear the message.

Gabriel explains that he will reveal what happens during the final stage of God's indignation, because the vision has a set time to end. God's judgment against His people's sins was real, but it had clear limits. The Lord remains completely in charge of both trials and deliverance.

Gabriel clearly states that the two-horned ram represents the kings of Media and Persia. The joined horns pictured how these two kingdoms united into one world empire. God named these nations in advance long before their history played out.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many critical scholars view the ram as Media alone rather than a combined Medo-Persian empire, arguing the book of Daniel was written after the events in the second century BC.

notes.meaning: The shaggy goat represents the kingdom of Greece, and the large horn between its eyes is its first king. This king was Alexander the Great, who united Greece and swept away the Persian Empire. Gabriel's direct words remove any doubt about who the symbols represent.

The four horns that replaced the broken one represent four kingdoms that sprang from Greece after Alexander's death. His empire was divided among four of his generals rather than passed down to his heirs. None of these four smaller kingdoms possessed the power or greatness that Alexander had.

Toward the end of those four kingdoms, when rebellion had reached its full measure, a shameless and deceitful king would arise. This foretells Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who was famous for cruelty and political trickery. God allowed him to come to power at a time when apostasy among the people had reached its peak.

differ.view: This ruler refers not only to Antiochus of old, but also points directly forward to the Antichrist.
The prophecy strictly describes Antiochus Epiphanes, and applying it directly to the Antichrist stretches the plain meaning of the text.

notes.meaning: This ruler gained great power, though his success was permitted by God rather than achieved by his own strength alone. He caused dreadful destruction and turned his anger against mighty leaders and God's holy people. His severe persecution tested the faith of the Jewish community to the limit.

Using clever schemes and false promises of peace, this king destroyed many people and grew exceedingly proud in his heart. He even dared to take a stand against the Prince of princes, the Lord God Almighty. Yet he was broken without human hands, dying of a sudden disease sent by God.

differ.view: The passage describes both Antiochus and the future Antichrist who directly opposes Christ.
The passage points directly and only to Antiochus Epiphanes during the Greek period.

notes.meaning: Gabriel assures Daniel that the revelation about the 2,300 evenings and mornings is true and reliable. Daniel is told to seal up the vision because its events were set for a distant time centuries later. God's promises can be trusted even when their fulfillment takes generations to arrive.

Daniel was completely worn out by what he saw and lay sick in bed for several days. After recovering, he got up and faithfully returned to his royal duties for the king. Even though he was troubled and could not fully grasp the vision, he continued to do his daily work for God.
